analysis.one_liner: Cracks down on foreclosure rescue and loan-modification scams by banning upfront fees.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees in June 2009 and never received a committee vote or floor vote before the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: During the foreclosure crisis, companies charged desperate homeowners big upfront fees for loan-modification or foreclosure-rescue help, then delivered little or nothing. This bill would have directed the Federal Trade Commission to write rules requiring written contracts with clear terms, a no-penalty cancellation window, and a ban on collecting any payment until services were actually performed and documented. State attorneys general could also sue violators in federal court. The bill never advanced past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners facing or fearing foreclosure, who were the prime targets of companies charging hundreds or thousands of dollars in advance for loan-modification help that often never materialized.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the FTC to write rules requiring any foreclosure rescue or loan modification service to use a written contract with clear disclosures about services, results, and total compensation [S2][S3].
Requires a clearly disclosed right to cancel within a set number of business days with no penalty or obligation [S2][S3].
Prohibits or restricts these services from collecting any money until services are fully performed, results achieved, and both documented to the homeowner [S2][S3].
Allows state attorneys general to sue violators in federal court to obtain injunctions, restitution, damages, and penalties, and to recover attorney fees if they prevail [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Foreclosure rescue and loan modification companies, which could no longer collect fees up front before performing any work, and would face FTC enforcement and state lawsuits for violations.

drawbacks.text: The bill relied on FTC rulemaking rather than banning the practices outright, and it excluded entities not subject to FTC enforcement, leaving gaps in coverage [S3].
The FTC could exempt entities from the rule if it determined including them was not necessary to prevent consumer injury, a discretion that could narrow protections [S3].
Stricter contracting and no-advance-fee rules could have added compliance costs for legitimate counselors and slowed some homeowners' access to paid modification assistance during the crisis.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections were targeted and modest: written contracts, a cancellation window, and no payment until work is done are standard consumer safeguards, and the bill preserved state laws without preemption. The main cost falls on a predatory niche industry; legitimate free or HUD-approved counseling was unaffected. On balance the benefits to at-risk homeowners outweighed the compliance costs.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to the Financial Services and Energy and Commerce committees, it went to a consumer protection subcommittee, and no committee or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Doris Matsui introduced the bill on June 2, 2009, joined by Rep. Gwen Moore, during the height of the foreclosure crisis [S1][S3].
It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day of introduction [S5].
One day later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection, and no further action was ever taken [S5].
The bill drew only one cosponsor and never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or Senate action before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S4][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies collecting upfront fees from homeowners for foreclosure rescue and loan modification help faced no new federal rules, and the FTC gained no new authority over them through this bill.

for.name: Rep. Doris Matsui
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require FTC rulemaking against upfront-fee foreclosure rescue and loan modification scams.

for.name: Rep. Gwen Moore
for.what_they_did: Joined Matsui in introducing the bill and appeared as its sole cosponsor.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill before the committee; after subcommittee referral no markup, vote, or further action occurred for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after its initial referral.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Democrats, so the bill's support was narrowly Democratic, but no recorded opposition exists either.

industries.industry: Foreclosure rescue and loan modification companies
industries.note: These firms charged homeowners fees up front for modification help and often delivered nothing; the bill would have barred advance payments and exposed them to FTC rules and state attorney general lawsuits. Their business model ran directly against the interest of homeowners in foreclosure.

The bill did not directly regulate servicers or lenders, but a functioning loan modification process could have increased workout volumes and reduced foreclosure losses for them. The effect is indirect either way.
